visual_habits.text: You photograph people inside their surroundings rather than close in on the face -- the setting is doing as much work as the subject.
visual_habits.evidence: 61 of 66 portraits put the face under 4% of the frame

visual_habits.text: You expose for the highlights and let the rest go dark. That is a choice a RAW file supports well, and it is why several of these open up in the edit.
visual_habits.evidence: 108 of 261 frames sit below a mean luminance of 100 of 255

technical_strengths.text: Your focus and your shutter discipline are reliable. Almost nothing here was lost to a technical failure.
technical_strengths.evidence: 257 of 261 frames carry no unrecoverable fault

technical_strengths.text: Your frames respond well to processing -- the gap between the file as shot and the file edited is real and consistent.
technical_strengths.evidence: a median of 7 points gained by a normal edit

artistic_strengths.text: Your frames hold together as whole pictures.
You leave things unresolved in the frame, which is what keeps a viewer in it.
Your pictures raise questions instead of listing what was present.

weaknesses.text: You shoot several near-identical frames of the same thing and keep them all. The extra takes are not adding a better version -- they are adding work later.
weaknesses.evidence: 53 of 261 frames lost to a sharper sibling

weaknesses.text: Expressions are being lost -- blinks and mid-word moments. This is a shooting rhythm problem, not an editing one.
The moments are general rather than particular -- there is often nothing happening that could only have happened then.
Horizons are coming in tilted often enough that it is worth fixing in the camera rather than in the crop -- straightening costs resolution every time.

improvements.text: Before you press the shutter on the obvious view, take two steps in any direction and look again. The frames here that stand out are the ones shot from somewhere other than where everyone stands.
improvements.evidence: distinctiveness averages 48 of 100 across the collection

improvements.text: Wait longer in the good light. Most of these frames record a place correctly; the strongest ones caught something happening in it.
Shoot the frame, then change something before shooting again -- move, wait, or change the angle. A second identical take cannot be better than the first.
improvements.evidence: 53 of 261 frames were near-duplicates of a better one
